clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive combined immunodeficiency caused by loss of DOCK2, a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor that governs actin remodelling and migration in lymphocytes and other leucocytes
Presents in early childhood with severe, recurrent, and invasive bacterial, viral, and fungal infections
Severe or disseminated viral disease, including herpesviruses and respiratory viruses, is a notable feature reflecting impaired antiviral immunity
Both T- and B-cell function are affected, with defective lymphocyte activation, migration, and antibody responses despite variable lymphocyte counts
Impaired natural killer cell and neutrophil function contributes to the breadth of infective susceptibility
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating the combined immune defect and confirming biallelic DOCK2 mutations by genetic testing

Because the disorder behaves as a severe combined immunodeficiency, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment, supported meanwhile by immunoglobulin replacement and antimicrobial prophylaxis
reference.pathophysiology: DOCK2 is a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor expressed mainly in haematopoietic cells that activates the small GTPase Rac, thereby controlling reorganisation of the actin cytoskeleton. This actin remodelling underlies many leucocyte functions: the migration of lymphocytes and neutrophils toward chemokines, the formation of the immunological synapse during T-cell activation, B-cell responses, and natural killer cell and interferon-driven antiviral defence. When DOCK2 is absent, lymphocytes and phagocytes cannot properly polarise, move, or signal, so adaptive and innate responses are broadly impaired. The result is a combined immunodeficiency in which affected children fail to contain bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens, with the antiviral deficit being especially prominent.
additionalDifferentials: Typical severe combined immunodeficiency of other genetic causes
Other actin-regulation or cytoskeletal immune defects
Combined immunodeficiencies with prominent viral susceptibility
additionalInvestigations: Lymphocyte subset enumeration with naive and memory T-cell analysis
Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses
Natural killer cell number and cytotoxicity testing
Assays of leucocyte migration and, where available, interferon responses
Microbiological and viral studies to identify and monitor infections
redFlags: Severe or disseminated viral infection in infancy
Recurrent invasive bacterial and fungal infections
Failure to thrive with early-onset severe infection
Lymphopenia or abnormal lymphocyte function on screening
A family history of early childhood death from infection or consanguinity
reference.prognosis: Untreated, the disorder carries a poor prognosis with early life-threatening infection; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the prospect of cure and is the treatment of choice, with outcomes best when undertaken early before infective damage accumulates.
pitfalls: Mistaking the picture for a purely antibody deficiency and delaying definitive treatment
Underestimating the antiviral defect and giving live vaccines
Attributing recurrent infection to environmental exposure rather than an inborn error
Delaying referral for transplantation while infections accumulate
Relying on lymphocyte counts alone, which may be misleadingly preserved
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
